speaker: The Chairman
text: Head N, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Mr Vikram Nair again.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It appears that this year, one of the most consequential factors is not just this relationship, but the new US administration's recalibration of almost all its international relationships.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Other than US and China, the major powers of the world may be considered the developed world countries, the nuclear powers as well as the G20 economies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Around the same time, tariffs were also threatened against the European Union (EU) countries, hitherto a close ally of the US in both economic and security matters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, US is Europe's largest trading partner and most EU countries are also a security ally of the US through the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Traditionally, US and Western Europe had been regarded as the "West", a group of generally philosophically aligned developed nations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It appears though that this alliance is now under pressure.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The differences on security matters have played out most starkly in positions on the war in Ukraine, with most European NATO allies condemning Russia's attack and supporting Ukraine's right of self-defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The US, which was hitherto, being an important supporter of the effort with provision of weapons to Ukraine, seems to now be more focused on a mineral deal with Ukraine and pressuring Ukraine to negotiate a peace deal that may involve giving up large parts of its territory, which was illegally conquered.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to China though, the US position does not seem to have changed significantly between the administrations in terms of direction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The new administration has announced a further increase in tariffs against selected goods from China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These may have less of a dramatic effect as the two countries' economies have already been decoupling since the initial round of tariffs launched more than a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, contestation between the two, especially on the technology front, has intensified.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The launch of DeepSeek has demonstrated China's artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, developed at a much lower cost than its counterparts in the US.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It appears the race is very much on between these two great powers on the technology front.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As US-China contestation intensifies, how has Singapore's ties with these major powers changed, and how has our role in the global landscape been affected?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What can Singapore do to manage these tensions?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, both the US and China are important partners of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We have had a long history of friendly relationships with both countries, with strategic cooperation in almost every sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The US has been Singapore's largest foreign direct investment partner, with investments in manufacturing, wholesale trade, finance and insurance.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: China is Singapore's biggest trading partner and Singapore is its largest foreign investor.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The US-China political and trade relations are at their lowest points in years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They have disagreements on many issues and in addition, rivalry has led to a very tense situation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How should Singapore chart our foreign policy amidst the US-China rivalry, given our close ties with both countries?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How can Singapore remain a relevant and trusted partner to both major countries?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, Singapore stands at a pivotal moment in our foreign relations, particularly in balancing our ties with the US and China.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As a small nation reliant on global stability, we must carefully navigate the intensifying competition between these two major powers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In 2024, we renewed a long-standing agreement that grants US military access to our facilities, further cementing our security partnership.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, our ties with China are deepening and continue to grow.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In 2023, the China-Singapore Free Trade Agreement was updated, enhancing cooperation in critical areas such as the digital economy and green technology.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Singapore is also China's largest foreign investor and plays a pivotal role in the Belt and Road Initiative.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The intensifying US-China rivalry over technologies like semi-conductors and artificial intelligence (AI) is creating significant uncertainty for businesses here.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Companies in Singapore are grappling with the complexities of navigating regulations and trade restrictions from both sides.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: China's actions in the South China Sea and its economic practices have sparked apprehension among some Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) countries.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, despite initiatives like the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework, uncertainties persist regarding the US' long-term commitment to the region.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Given the increasingly complex global landscape, how can Singapore continue to strengthen our bilateral relations with both the US and China, while safeguarding our independence and advancing our national interests?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chairman, there is a troubling resurgence of big power contestation and the rising possibility of a hot war with leaders who appear increasingly dismissive of international laws and norms.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: History reminds us that powerful nations have always vied for influence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the speed and intensity of today's power plays are unprecedented.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this volatile environment, smaller states like Singapore cannot afford to be complacent.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just look at what happened in the Oval Office last week.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must remember that when great powers collide, smaller nations must keep their wits, or risk being trampled.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For a small but open economy like ours, every disruption at sea, in the air, or even in boardrooms, echoes across our island.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our sovereignty depends on the global community honouring international laws.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If might becomes right, smaller states will find themselves squeezed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The gradual erosion of long-standing norms casts an ominous shadow over our national security.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Peace, after all, is delicate; we cannot let the heavy footprints of great powers tread on our Independence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Amid the shifting calculus of the circles of power in Washington, Beijing, Moscow and beyond, we must stand ready for sudden turns in policy, whether in technology alliances or strategic supply chains.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because in a fluid world where alliances can form and fracture overnight, vigilance and self-reliance are our strongest shields.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore's reliability stems from abiding by international law and seeking peaceful resolution of disputes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We continue to nurture strong ties with our partners, while fortifying ASEAN unity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A cohesive regional bloc protects our shared interests and dampens external pressures.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, Singaporeans must also realise how vital it is to avoid reflexively choosing sides.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That could serve another power's agenda rather than Singapore's.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A well-informed, united citizenry is our frontline in foreign policy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When we collectively understand the rationale behind our diplomatic stances, we become a nation that speaks with one voice and stands firm amidst the chaos.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this epoch of renewed big power contests, Singapore's path must be clear: remain steadfast in our principles, unwavering in our commitment to international law, and yet astute in balancing relationships with all of our partners, big or small.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We may be small, but we must stand tall, guided by the power of principle over the principle of power.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must stand behind our Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) officers who work tirelessly to secure Singapore's place in a world increasingly turned on its head.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How do we therefore navigate the complex global landscape becomes ever more important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How does MFA assess our place in this contested landscape?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And how do we prepare Singaporeans for the New World Order?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because when the storms of geopolitics rage, Singapore will and must stay resolute, for that is how small states like ours stand our ground.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, as tensions between the US and China remain unresolved, businesses and Singaporeans are concerned about the broader implications on trade, investment and security.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry provide an update on Singapore's efforts to navigate these challenges, particularly in maintaining our relevance as a neutral and strategic partner to both the US and China, ensuring continued trade access and investment flows?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How is MFA strengthening diplomatic and economic engagements to safeguard Singapore's interests amidst increasing global fragmentation?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a small state with an open economy, Singapore is highly vulnerable to disruptions from this great power competition.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Balancing strong military and economic ties with the US with deep economic links with China requires careful diplomacy, strategic autonomy and economic adaptability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Changes in US engagement in Asia and rising military tensions with China create new security challenges for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To strengthen its defence resilience, Singapore should strengthen its defence partnership with the US while expanding security cooperation with more countries, including some of our neighbours in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, Singapore must continue building up the capability and competence of the Singapore Armed Forces to ensure it remains a credible deterrent against emerging threats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Building diplomatic goodwill through bilateral engagement and assistance will also be important in winning international support for Singapore in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MFA should expand efforts to educate businesses, non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and the public about our strategic interest through town halls and closed hall closed door briefings.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It can also make better use of social media, podcasts and short videos to ensure foreign policy messaging reaches wider domestic and international audiences.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister outline what MFA is doing in these areas and how it plans to strengthen its such efforts?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, multilateralism has been the cornerstone of our world since the end of World War II.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The United Nations, along with the Bretton Woods institutions of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank were the key pillars of a world where major powers acknowledged that this was the best hope for a more prosperous and secure world for everyone.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This was followed by a proliferation of multilateral treaties on a wide range of matters over the decades as countries found more and more areas to cooperate on.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore, like many other countries, prospered against this backdrop and is party to a large network of multilateral and bilateral treaties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In my opening cut, I had discussed how the US seems to be redefining its relationships with both its NAFTA and NATO allies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What is the impact of these moves on international co-operation to tackle issues such as pandemics and climate change, and how can small states like Singapore prevent a weakening of the international rules-based order?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Chairman, Singapore's prosperity depends on a stable and rules-based international system.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: As global discussions evolve in areas like AI, cybersecurity, and climate change, how is Singapore ensuring that our national interests are protected at multilateral fora?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: What steps are we taking, to stay actively engaged with key international partners so that we remain influential in shaping policies that impact us?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Given that international law is crucial for a small trade-dependent nation like ours, how is Singapore contributing to efforts to uphold global rules and safeguard our long-term security and economic interests?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, since the end of World War II, the world has benefited from a stable rules-based international order.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a result, the relative peace and order in most parts of the world have enabled development and economic growth, uplifting millions from poverty and raising the standards of living for people around the globe.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a small state with no natural resources and whose economy is highly dependent on trade, Singapore has benefited greatly from the conducive global environment brought about by the rules-based international order too.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since our Independence 60 years ago, Singapore has been a keen supporter of globalisation and free trade.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have also participated actively in international organisations, such as the UN and the World Trade Organization.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These have fostered Singapore's economic advances and national development over the years and contributed to higher living standards and prosperity for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, the global environment is now changing, with the rules-based international order under immense stress from developments, such as the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, tensions in the Middle East and recent tariff conflicts.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These developments are detrimental to the interests of small states like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Against this backdrop, what is Singapore doing to support the upholding of the rules-based international order which is under tremendous stress?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With declining support for globalisation, how are we supporting international bodies that promote globalisation which is critical for Singapore's survival and prosperity?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, since the World War II, countries around the world have largely operated under a set of principles, norms, rules and agreements and where nations' sovereignties are respected.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The current state of international affairs and the worrying recent developments have, however, severely threatened this rules-based global order and thrust countries like Singapore into this unchartered territory.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Are we seeing the erosions of multilateralism and fraying of the rules-based global order?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How has Singapore contributed to the Pact for the Future and how will Singapore continue to contribute to strengthening multilateralism?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Chairman, since 1965, our core foreign policy has served us well through three distinctive periods in the international world order.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The first was the Cold War, a time when global world power was divided into fixed blocs of influence, with parts of Southeast Asia mired in active conflicts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The second came after the fall of the Berlin Wall, ushering in a unipolar world dominated by the United States, where globalisation and free trade became the defining aspects of international relations.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, the world is going through a phase of greater contestation, fragmentation and bifurcation on the global stage.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This was born out of a fundamental lack of strategic trust between the major powers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: A number of countries are also turning to protectionist and nationalist policies, as they become more insular in their outlook and transactional in their foreign policy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: These developments are detrimental to international trade, relations and cooperation among nations, especially for important issues which we need to work together on, like climate change.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Singapore has consistently sought to play a constructive and relevant role on the global stage.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: As a small nation-state and open economy highly dependent on global trade, we need to do our best to join hands with countries with similar outlooks on mutual cooperation and partnerships.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: To better safeguard Singapore's interest, can MFA share how we have been able to build ties with like-minded partners to expand our common interest and amplify our voice and impact in the international arena?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, not too many years ago, it was put to us that "a small nation has no foreign policy".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The corollary, of course, is that "might makes right"; big countries will do what they can, while small countries will suffer what they must.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Fast forward a few years, these cardinal instincts of big countries are manifesting more and more in our geopolitical realities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Where there was once polite restraint and a basic respect for rules tempered by enlightened self-interest, we now find increasingly naked, unbridled hegemony and hubris.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We now see a big country invading a small country on the basis of historical errors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We see big countries laying claim on the resources and territories of small countries.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We see a big country reminding a small country of its place in life, putting a small country in its place in front of world media in the most public of settings.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And we see big countries dealing with one another, bargaining with one another on the fate of a small country, where the small country is on the table, not at the table.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, it feels like the world order, as we have known it for the last three decades, is not fraying at the edges; but rather, breaking down from the centre.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, how is a small state like Singapore to face and survive in this new world order?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How can we go about maximising strategic space for ourselves in this jungle?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And how do we secure our destiny going forward?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Specifically, how can Singapore work even more closely with fellow small states around the world to find strength in numbers and secure our collective future, together?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, the US has been an important ally of Singapore on multiple fronts, including on trade, investments and defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: We have been a reliable ally of the US in this region since our Independence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Our forces have regular training exercises with the US.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: According to MFA, we have cooperation on many other fronts with the US, including people-to-people exchanges, cooperation on climate, space, critical technologies and cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Have any of these wide-ranging areas of cooperation been affected by the change in the US administration?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This incident has cast Singapore in a negative light as a potential backdoor for US tech leakage.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What is Singapore doing to manage and correct such perceptions?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Chairman, as the second Trump administration takes shape, Singapore must navigate an evolving geopolitical landscape while maintaining our strong and longstanding partnership with America.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: We host significant US fixed asset investments, with many US companies using Singapore to serve the region.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Our deep economic interests, ties, defence cooperation and collaborations in areas like finance, trade and technology, have provided a strong foundation for bilateral relations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: However, the US' shifting global priorities, differing approaches to trade and taxation, and increasing competition in critical technologies introduce new complexities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As global supply chains and digital infrastructure become even more strategically sensitive, ensuring continued trust and cooperation will be key.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: What are some of the areas that we hope to continue to pursue?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: How can Singapore maintain the trust of the US, especially in potentially sensitive areas, such as cybersecurity, advanced technologies and innovation?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore and the US share a strong and multifaceted relationship, and this has grown over many decades.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The bilateral ties between our two countries are defined by strong economic, defence, innovation and people-to-people connections.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In line with its current trade policy, the US has demonstrated a readiness to impose new tariffs on various countries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As a small and open economy, Singapore is susceptible to global supply chain disruptions and trade tensions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What potential impact can such tariffs, direct or indirect, have on Singapore?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How can we strategically position ourselves to mitigate this impact?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.26 pm until 3.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In particular, how might shifts in US foreign policy, especially its intensifying rivalry with China, along with changes in economic priorities and trade policies, affect key areas of cooperation, such as defence, trade and technology partnerships?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a small but globally connected nation, Singapore must carefully balance its relationships with key partners, including the US, China, Europe, ASEAN and other major economies, amidst global fragmentation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How is the Government ensuring that Singapore strengthens its international ties while upholding a calibrated, independent foreign policy that safeguards our national interests?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Today, as China shifts towards high-tech innovation and sustainable growth, Singapore's expertise in finance, governance and smart city solutions offers new synergies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: What are the areas where Singapore and China share complementary advantages and can work together to benefit the region?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In a multicultural society like ours, differing perspectives on foreign affairs can easily upset our hard-won racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the global geopolitical landscape grows more complex and fragmented, it is more important than ever for Singaporeans to stay cohesive in our approach.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, in recent times, information is increasingly consumed through social media and messaging apps whose algorithms reinforce specific viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a result, the public is less exposed to diverse perspectives than in the past, when traditional media offered a broader range of views.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can MFA share how it fosters public understanding and national consensus on Singapore's foreign policy priorities?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Despite the growing US-China rivalry, Singapore has remained consistent and principled in our engagement with both powers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, these international norms are increasingly being challenged and tensions between the two major economies continue to escalate.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given this shifting geopolitical climate, how is Singapore working to deepen our cooperation with China while maintaining our strategic autonomy?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What are our strategies to strengthen bilateral cooperation and people-to-people ties amidst these geopolitical uncertainties?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: At the same time, competition for both material and non-material resources, like highly skilled manpower in specialised fields, has intensified.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Against this backdrop, how can we safeguard Singapore's interests on the international stage and secure the necessary resources, maintain ties, mutual support and cooperation with our partners?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How can Singapore ensure that we remain at the forefront in emerging areas, such as AI, cyberspace, digital economy, green economy and outer space, and promote cooperation in these areas?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: But we must be wondering what MFA got to do with all these?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As MFA plays a crucial role in global diplomacy, strengthening international partnerships in critical areas of technology is vital.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: By engaging with like-minded countries and multinational corporations, we can create avenues for knowledge sharing, joint ventures and access to new markets.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: How can we maintain Singapore's competitive edge on frontier issues, especially on critical and emerging technologies, and ensure that we continue to be an attractive hub for investment and R&D?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Critical and cutting-edge sectors, such as AI, biotechnology and quantum computing, will define the future of industries worldwide.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Our challenge, therefore, is not only to keep pace with these developments but to position ourselves as a global leader in these fields.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve this, we must focus on three key areas – fostering innovation, strengthening international partnerships and creating a conducive environment for investment and R&D.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, maintaining our competitive edge on frontier issues is essential to Singapore's future success.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Let us continue to be a global leader in technological innovation and an attractive hub for investment and research.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is one of our numerous bilateral events to strengthen our ties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is heartening to note that our countries are committed to deepening our cooperation across more areas which will benefit citizens of both nations, including connectivity, trade, investment, culture, education, digitalisation and sustainability.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on the current state of Singapore-Malaysia relations and what are some of the key initiatives to further enhance bilateral cooperation, especially as both sides commemorate the 60th anniversary of bilateral relations this year?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: As close neighbours, our relations with Malaysia are built on a strong foundation of mutual trust and win-win cooperation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Could MFA share what are some of the other key areas covered at the 11th Malaysia-Singapore Leaders' Retreat and what other areas are both sides committed to cooperate on?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: We have had a long-standing and close historic relationship with Indonesia and were both founding members of ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: These agreements were negotiated between teams led by Senior Minister Teo Cheen Hean for Singapore and Indonesia's Coordinating Minister for Maritime Affairs and Investments, Mr Luhut Binsar Pandjaitan.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This was signed at the leaders retreat and witnessed by then-Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong and President Jokowi.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: These agreements resolved and provided clarity on some long-standing matters in our bilateral relationship.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In October last year, President Prabowo was sworn-in as Indonesia's new President.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, this is a more sombre, a more careful and a brutally frank message this year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The common thread in all the intervention so far has been this big question: has the post-World War Two liberal world order come to an end?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is a world order which has prevailed for eighty years.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In 2025, Singapore celebrates our 60th anniversary, but it is also the 80th anniversary of the end of the Second World War.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In these six decades, successive generations of hardworking and disciplined Singaporeans have built up our tiny city-state into an outstanding beacon of economic and social success.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That we did so without any natural resources or past fiscal reserves is all the more remarkable.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But we should also be realistic and humble enough to be cognisant that there were external factors that were very conducive to our success.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The post-World War liberal world order was characterised by first, the proliferation and the rise of free trade and global supply chains and multinational enterprises; second, the establishment of multilateral institutions, United Nations, the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the World Trade Organization (WTO) for trade, and the World Health Organization (WHO) for health; third, the development of international law and the treaties to protect the global commons, including, for instance, the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea, the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, the Treaty for Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdictions (BBNJ).

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This world order was initially envisioned and underwritten by the US and supported by its transatlantic allies in Western Europe.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In turn, it was boosted by the reform and opening (改革开放) in China, under Mr Deng Xiaoping, since 1978.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The economic liberalisation of India under Prime Minister Narasimha Rao since 1991; and the integration of ASEAN economies, especially at the end of the Cold War, when Indochina joined us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This global order was very favourable for a tiny city-state, which has a trade volume three times our gross domestic product (GDP); and Singapore's role as a global financial centre and our business ecosystem, with intensive interactions between local and foreign companies engaged in advanced manufacturing and the provision of sophisticated services for a global market.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In a sense, the point I am making is that Singapore enjoyed the best of many worlds and we were able to go to fire on all cylinders.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And this is a global change, not just in one place.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The big powers are taking a narrower view of their national interests and they are adopting a more transactional, frankly sometimes, even more coercive approach.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And because there is a lack of strategic trust between the big powers, each of them has deep anxiety to stay ahead of each other.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These profound shifts have ushered in an era of sharper rivalry, autarky and the fracturing of global supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Countries have turned inwards, ostensibly in the name of national security, resilience and de-risking in order to secure their individual interests in this turbulent environment.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is not merely a sudden temporary change in diplomatic weather.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The question then is what does this portend for us in Singapore?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is a question on all your minds.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There are three broad sets of implications for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US, for a very long time, was the main advocate for freer trade globally.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is a completely understandable political question for the domestic American voter to say, why should the US continue to unilaterally underwrite this liberal world order which, in fact, has brought peace and prosperity for so many other countries around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And so, over the last decade, the US has progressively shifted to a more nationalist approach, in response to what it deems to be unfair trade measures and free riding.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The new US administration clearly sees tariffs as a means to address non-trade-related policy objectives, including national security, local job creation, more resilient supply chains and bargaining leverage.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Other major countries are also using similar restrictions on trade more frequently, and not always confining themselves to trade-related issues.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Tariffs are being applied to partners, competitors and adversaries alike.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US has announced tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China, and in turn, these countries have also signalled retaliatory measures.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Tit-for-tat tariffs by other countries could easily escalate into a global trade war.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But even if we are not, we will still be affected.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These tariffs will have a major impact on the volume and patterns of world trade and significantly affect us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The first level, as a transshipment hub and with all the other global services that we provide to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There will be supply chain disruptions, there will be more volatile prices.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And it is worth remembering, if you cast your mind back to the 1930s, the Great Depression, retaliatory “beggar-thy-neighbour” policies, in fact, slowed growth rates everywhere.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, we need to be prepared for this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But the problems go beyond just trade and tariffs.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Because, in fact, there are also implications on the global financial systems and the way frontier technology, which some of the Members have referred to, is being developed, is being shared and is being exploited.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In a sense, all these levers, tariffs, financial systems and technology may be weaponised.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Because Singapore operates as an open economy that is deeply integrated with all the big powers around the world, we trade, invest and access technologies from all of them.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are a vital node in a global network.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Singapore model is built on trust, openness and a level playing field.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We allow companies from all over the world to operate here as long as they play by the rules.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Unfortunately, technology has become a focal point for strategic contestation between the big powers.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And as countries bid to stay ahead, several have imposed restrictions and export controls on semi-conductor chips, critical minerals and on data.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And amidst the heightened scrutiny over advanced technology, Singapore may be criticised for working with or hosting companies and officials from one side or the other, or both.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There will be centrifugal pressure from all sides that will make it increasingly hard for us to operate and it will threaten our raison d’être as an open hub.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The second set of implications is on war and peace.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Russia-Ukraine war has now entered its fourth year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In its immediate aftermath, global energy and food prices surged, and this worsened global inflation in 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Russia cited “historical errors” and “crazy decisions” to justify an invasion and to annex territory of its smaller neighbour.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As a tiny city state that has been independent for only 60 years, this immediately rang alarm bells for us in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have known the Russian Foreign Minister for quite a long time, so we have very open conversations.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And in 2022, I explained to him that because of Singapore’s circumstances, we had to uphold the principles of sovereign equality and territorial integrity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Similarly, I had a telephone conversation with my counterpart from Ukraine, Andrii Sybiha, last week.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Not about the details, the operational details, but about why this was happening.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And he told me, and I am paraphrasing, that this war was about his country’s sovereignty, his country’s territorial integrity and freedom to choose how to organise a society and to have a closer strategic relationship with Europe.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And then, for good measure, he added laconically, “and our critical minerals”.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both Russia and Ukraine, and I have taken pains to emphasise that all my interactions with the foreign ministers, know that Singapore is upholding principles and we are not taking sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Europeans and Americans initially responded forcefully to defend Ukraine and to isolate Russia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But recent pronouncements and actions by the new US administration, most recently, the dramatic live video from the Oval Office, have dramatically underlined a change in long-standing US policy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is now clear that the trans-Atlantic relationship is under severe strain and NATO members are now seriously and urgently rethinking their strategic and security situation and their policy options.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, meetings are going on even now as we speak.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: After the failure of the security guarantees for Ukraine that were given in 1994 in exchange for giving up its nuclear weapons.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Closer home, tensions in the South China Sea, through which one-third of global trade passes through, continue to simmer.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Taiwan Strait remains a potential flashpoint and we all know that tensions have increased in recent years.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: All these global developments, on both the economic and geostrategic fronts, have profound implications for us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: International law, the UN Charter, the principles of sovereign equality, political independence, and territorial integrity have all been severely eroded.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We may, in fact, be reverting to a time when the world is divided into blocs controlled by big powers.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And by definition, this must mean the loss of choice and autonomy for small states.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I recall a speech that Mr Lee Kuan Yew gave back in 1973, the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: He referred to an old African proverb, that “when elephants fight, the grass suffers”.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But he added one additional line, “and when elephants make love, it is disastrous.” I would not go through the powerful imagery, but the point is, when big powers are on the move, for whatever reason, it is a dangerous time for the rest of us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Third implication is our ability to respond collectively to global threats and safeguard the global commons has been significantly impaired.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The collective commitment to international institutions such as the WTO and WHO as well as compliance with international treaties like the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement that resulted from it, are all waning.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Imagine, is the world today in a better state to deal with another pandemic, given a severely weakened WHO, and how are we going respond to climate change if we do not have the institutions and the processes to protect the global commerce?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our foreign policy begins at home and it must always be a balance between realism and idealism.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It means that we must have no illusions about our place in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But small as we are, for 60 years, we have refused to adopt a fatalistic posture.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have insisted on agency to build our strength, to protect our sovereignty, maintain our relevance and to create political and economic space for ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We strive to be useful, but not to be made use of.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And of course, to avoid becoming a sacrificial pawn between big powers.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have dwelt at length on the dangers arising from the end of the previous world order.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The point is I am making an appeal for us all to be alert, to be realistic and to be careful in dangerous times.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But a note of caution is not a call for pessimism because, in fact, Singapore has good reason to have confidence in our future, due to the pioneering work of our past generations.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Because of our strength economically, we cannot be bullied or bought.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have significant national reserves, and if the biggest criticism that we face in this Budget is budget marksmanship and having more reserves than we had anticipated, I think that is a reason for celebration, considering the circumstances in which we are going into.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: On the international stage, if you have to put your hand out for assistance, it means you have no say.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is a big advantage for Singapore not to have to beg for aid.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have no need for assistance or loans that will subject us to external pressure.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are not dependent on any single external partner.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And perhaps even more importantly, and you have just heard Minister Ng's speech earlier, we do not depend on any external country to defend Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have the capability and the will to defend ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For six decades, we have invested fiscal resources, approved by Parliament, and every man in this Chamber and his son has served National Service.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The fact that everybody knows that we are good for our money and we put our blood where we stand on, is the core of deterrence and respect.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But all this is not enough if we did not have unity at home, and we need to live up to the pledge to be one united people, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And on this note, I want to thank the Opposition that so far, we have worked on the basis that politics stops at the water's edge, and our diplomacy works because we have painstakingly forged and maintain domestic consensus on our core long-term interest in foreign policy priorities.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our diversity in Singapore does mean that from time to time, Singaporeans will have different views on developments around the world, and we have to provide space for this diversity to be expressed, but without letting it become a means to divide us as a country.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: A clear example is the disaster in Gaza.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is a deeply emotional issue and many Singaporeans feel very deeply about this, have expressed a range of emotions, and sometimes, even conflicting emotions on this point.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When we make our foreign policy decisions, we do so on the basis of national interest.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And the reason why we have to be so categorical is because if Singapore was ever attacked in this way – and the risks are not zero – but if Singapore was ever attacked in this way, we too would certainly exercise our right of self-defence to the full.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And it is why that in the aftermath of that attack we had strongly reaffirmed the right to self-defence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: You see, in the case of both Ukraine and Hamas, we took positions for our own sake, for our own national interest, and not because we were taking sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we say all this because it is in our national interest for international law to be upheld and not to be flouted.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Funds are being collected, even now in this month, the holy month of Ramadan.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: You heard Minister Ng explain that we make the extra effort to deliver these supplies through the Republic of Singapore Air Force.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is crucial, therefore, that we stay united and keep being able to adopt this collective constructive approach, even when we have different views to events and tragedies far from our shores.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And a deeper reason why we need to do this is because if conflict broke out nearer to us, in Asia, it will not only have even greater emotional resonance, it will have a larger economic impact and it will also elicit a range of reaction from our people, and it will be even harder to manage.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is also worth remembering that there will always be external actors who will try to influence the views of our people and take advantage of our diversity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, long before the onset of kinetic action, we must expect grey zone tactics to be used to divide and polarise our people.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We can have different views, but we will stay united and we will close ranks on issues of national interest, so that we can ultimately secure what is best for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: How are we going to engage the world and our partners in this rapidly changing landscape, given that we are not sure where the next conflict or consummation of a condominium between big powers will occur.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And as Minister Ng put it, a very stark reminder, if anyone says they know exactly what is going to happen next, that shows a very dangerous delusion.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: You do not know what is going to happen next, but you know that we are living in dangerous times.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, fundamentally, our foreign policy must continue to be anchored by long-standing principles that have kept us afloat for six decades, even whilst we make tactical adjustments, or even strategic adjustments to our approach.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must maintain an omni-directional, a balance and a constructive engagement with all partners.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Yes, I know is going to be more difficult when they are quarrelling with each other, but in fact, all the more important, we have to work at it.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is our top trading partner in services.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is our third largest trading partner in goods.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And on the defence front, Minister Ng has already explained to you, how we are the US' only major security cooperation partner and we have a mutually beneficial relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Many of our companies are invested in China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, according to China's statistics, Singapore is their largest foreign investor.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And of course, we have strong people-to-people ties, historical and cultural ties.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both the US and China are also at the frontier of many leading technologies, whether it be AI, biotechnology or green energy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must be able to continue to work with both of them and ensure that our relations are mutually beneficial.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will never be the largest trading or strategic partner to either China or the US, basically, because we are a small country, but we can be amongst their most reliable and consistent partners.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And that is valuable and appreciated by both of them.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have maintained our relevance and credibility with both powers by being consistent, by being transparent and being constructive.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We do not simply tell them what they want to hear, but we are principled, we are trustworthy and we play a straight game.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And both of them know that when Singapore takes a stand, it is not because we are doing it at the behest of its rival, of its adversary, but that we take a stand because we have done our own calculation of what is in our long-term enlightened national interest.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Moving on to our immediate neighbourhood, we must continue to strengthen our ties in our region, bilaterally, especially and most intensively, with Malaysia and Indonesia, and obviously with ASEAN.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will continue to do so on the basis of interdependency, mutual respect and aim to build healthy relations, which will be crucial for stability and growth of our entire region.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Vikram Nair has asked about the state of our relations with Malaysia and Indonesia, respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I think we all know there is much to be gained by working together constructively with your most immediate neighbours.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: With Malaysia, we continue to work on the delimitation of our maritime boundaries.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There is still some areas there to be settled.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are negotiating on airspace and on water.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim have committed to not allow any single issue to overshadow our overall positive agenda.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we are pursuing mutually beneficial projects, both bilaterally and regionally, to strengthen connections and connectivity for the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Fortunately for us, he is familiar with Singapore and we have been able to work well with him.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are making good progress, including in areas like renewable energy, human capital development and particularly, in the fields of education and healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked how we can ensure ASEAN's continued relevance and centrality.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is worth remembering that ASEAN was founded in 1967 on the principle that either we hang together or we will be hung separately.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It was forged in a time when Southeast Asia was an arena for proxy wars during the Cold War period, and ASEAN's founder members were the non-communist part of Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Given that we are now entering another dangerous volatile phase, this concept of hanging together has just become even more salient.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: ASEAN, so far, has been able to maintain regional peace and stability, and enabled all of us collectively to focus on economic growth and in particular, economic integration.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: All member states are concerned about the wider geopolitical developments and the intensifying contestation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And ASEAN's convening power will remain relevant and important in the years ahead, to ensure that whilst we do not want to be an arena for proxy wars, we do want to be a safe harbour where all powers will have a stake in our success, and that we can maximise opportunities and autonomy for ASEAN member states.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Beyond our immediate neighbourhood, it is also crucial for us to make common cause with as many partners as possible, including India, Japan, the Middle East, Africa, Europe, Latin America, Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific Islands.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: My counterparts from some of these other countries have shared that they, too, are concerned about the impact of increasing contestation and rising protectionism.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They, too, would prefer a world that is open and committed to trade.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This means that even though free trade has had a setback, we can still make common cause with those who believe it is a formula for mutual peace and prosperity, and we have got to keep that flame going.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, for instance, Members may or may not be aware that we have been able to sign new trade agreements in the last few years.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For instance, Mercosur in 2023, which is Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay; and the Pacific Alliance, which is Peru, Chile, Mexico, Columbia, in 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If you actually pay attention to these countries, in fact, their elections have thrown up a very wide diversity of political parties, but they have all been keen to do free trade agreements with us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We believe this will expand markets and increase opportunities for us in Latin America.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are also pressing ahead on the digital economy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore, New Zealand and Chile signed the Digital Economy Partnership Agreement in 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We agreed to elevate relations with India to a comprehensive strategic partnership and we are well-poised to participate in India's growth potential.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: With Australia, we are setting an ambitious agenda for the next phase of our comprehensive strategic partnership, which will be refreshed this year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It will cover cooperation in emerging areas like AI, biotechnology and renewable energy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will also elevate our enhanced partnership with New Zealand.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will continue to work closely with Japan which remains committed to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) and to closer economic ties.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: With the Republic of Korea, we are working to upgrade relations to a strategic partnership later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have also upgraded relations with the UK and Germany to a strategic partnership and we are working to enhance relations with France to a comprehensive strategic partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our relations with the Gulf are also robust.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This year, we signed an MOU establishing a Strategic Partnership Council with Saudi Arabia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Last October, we had eight MOUs with the United Arab Emirates in social development, leadership development, AI and civilian nuclear energy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are also stepping up engagement of Africa, a centre of growth for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, as you can see, we have been working very hard on this strong, wide network of partners with whom we can trade, invest, do business with and engage in constructive partnerships on these emerging issues.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Not bad, considering the zeitgeist of our times.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: At the UN, we continue to be a staunch advocate for multilateralism, for adherence to international law, for the importance of the UN Charter.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This system is vital for countries, big and small, in order for us to have a chance to compete on a level playing field.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong and Mr Mark Lee have asked about this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore must and will remain a strong supporter of multilateralism.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will make common cause and we will stand up for this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is why we established the Forum of Small States (FOSS) back in 1992, which now has 108 members.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, this is a majority of members of the UN.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: FOSS is a platform to foster closer cooperation, reinforce multilateralism and support the developmental aspirations of small states.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we will continue to strengthen and improve the existing international architecture and ensure that it is fit-for-purpose.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This was a significant milestone for the international community.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It demonstrated that the UN is still, from time to time, against great difficulty, able to arrive at consensus and able to advance the agenda for collective good.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Without UNCLOS and the right of transit passage, Singapore would effectively be "sea-locked".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, it is a crucial plank of international law for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Despite the challenges, with patient and skillful diplomacy, the point I am trying to make is that it is still possible to arrive at international agreements by consensus.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Another recent example was the adoption of the treaty on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ).

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our Ambassador Rena Lee presided over the inter-governmental conference.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I hope all Members will support this nomination as well.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must actively create opportunities that will enable Singapore to be a magnet for ideas, technology, talent and capital.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Neil Parekh and Ms Poh Li San have asked how we can do this, especially in critical and emerging technology, and given the contestation between the big powers.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We already have actively advanced cooperation with a range of like-minded partners on emerging technology.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This includes our partners like the US, China, India, UK, Japan, Germany, France and Australia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We remain clear-eyed that there is strategic contestation between the major powers and it does complicate our attempts to create an open platform.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Nevertheless, we remain plugged into international conversations on technology standards and norm settings, in line with our own national interests.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our permanent representative to the UN in New York, Mr Burhan Gafoor, serves as the chairman of the UN Open-ended Working Group on security of and in the use of information and communications technology (ICT).

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That means he has to work intensively with the entire international community to advance policy discussions, norms and generate practical solutions to preserve international peace and security in cyberspace and maximise opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Members can imagine that during a time of fractures, to be able to engage all parties and to make progress, no matter how difficult it is, is a major achievement, and he deserves full credit for it.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Domestically, our strong rule of law and trust in our system will be crucial if we want to be able to attract and retain technology and, I need to emphasise, talent from all over the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore cannot afford to exclude anyone, any technology, any company with access to frontier ideas, frontier technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For that, I also need to make an appeal.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Of course, we will prioritise the interests of Singaporeans, but if we are going to seize the opportunity in frontier technologies, we need to be prepared to complement the Singaporean team, the Singaporean workforce, in order to gain access to ideas and technology.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But having said that, everyone who comes here and any company operating here, wherever you are from, will have to play by the rules.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I think two weeks ago, I explained, we will take firm action and move decisively against errant individuals and companies that flout our domestic laws.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We do not condone companies taking advantage of their association with us to engage in evasive, deceptive or dubious business practices for short-term commercial advantages, because that actually sullies and takes unfair advantage of Singapore's reputation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, Members may read, in the coming days, in the news on certain developments on this front.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But I need Members to understand that we are doing so to protect our standing as a trusted, open hub, painstakingly built-up over decades.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is how we have kept ourselves an attractive destination for leading companies with technology from all over the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must remain open to top talent and, as I said just now, to complement Team Singapore, because then, we can take maximal advantage of the opportunities which are emerging in this world that is unfolding in front of us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are at the end of an era.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The interregnum is likely to be chaotic, difficult, dangerous and tumultuous.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore and Singaporeans, every one of us will need to be realistic, to be careful and to be nimble.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But the point is, we do have strengths and there are opportunities ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I want to end by thanking all Members for their unstinting support for the work of all our diplomats who have been working so hard all over the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: (In Mandarin):   During the Lunar New Year period, I attended many "loh-hei" events.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At such functions, we would usually chat about current affairs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This year, there were many topics of discussion concerning global developments, including China-US relations, political changes in Europe, and the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The hottest topic was the US Presidential election and subsequent developments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: On the whole, the Chinese community shared fairly positive assessments of Trump 2.0.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I believe this is because many active members of Chinese community groups are businesspeople, who believe the current President to be pro-business.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Some also admire his unconventional political style and relentless pace of change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Chinese community leaders I had met agreed that all was not quite well with the world, but did not display much anxiety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Of course, people did notice that the raising of tariffs has become a new normal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The US, which had long been the main advocate for freer trade has changed its stance, and now employs tariffs and non-tariff barriers in pursuit of economic and non-economic objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Even then, because Singapore was not a direct target of these tariffs, my friends in the Chinese community expressed hope that Singapore would not be too affected by the global situation, including possible trade wars.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There were two other hopes: First, that the war in Ukraine would end soon, leading to more stable energy and food prices globally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, that no matter what, the world would need a place like Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These conversations took place about two weeks ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Since then, more drastic changes have taken place on the world stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Even those who felt relatively unperturbed 2 weeks ago may start to feel uneasy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: First, the impact of global developments on Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The US has announced tariffs on Canada, Mexico, and China, which in turn have signalled retaliatory measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Risks of a global trade war have increased.
