speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Beyond trade and tariffs, our economic model will also face serious challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Despite being a small country without natural resources or a hinterland, a stable rules-based international trading system has enabled Singapore to create prosperity through pursuing an open economic policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: A clear instance is how technology has become a focal point for strategic contestation between the big powers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This means we have to work harder to secure opportunities for prosperity and success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, the implications of war and peace on Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Over the past three years, two major conflicts – the war in Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East – have seen the loss of countless lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The conflict in the Middle East in particular has resulted in a humanitarian disaster that tugs at the heartstrings of many Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Russian-Ukraine war has exacerbated energy and food price hikes and caused long-term impacts on inflation and business costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Middle East situation, particularly developments in the Red Sea had impacted global shipping costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is therefore understandable that businesspeople in our Chinese community hope for these wars to end and for business costs to moderate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Alas, peace seems more remote than ever before.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Recent events have signified major shifts in geopolitics, with possibly unbridgeable differences emerging between the US and Europe on how to end the Ukraine war, and indeed, the global security architecture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Prospects for Ukraine have become even more grim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Even as we prepare for continued turbulence in the world, these changes have profound implications for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The idea that military aggression can force a country to compromise on its sovereignty and political independence would set a dangerous precedent for countries worldwide, particularly small countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Unfortunately, we are witnessing the weakening of international norms and the rise of the law of the jungle, or "might is right".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The price of national autonomy and self-determination has increased significantly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This means painful choices and immense pressure for many countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For example, some allies of the US that had depended on American security guarantees are now grappling with cutting expenditure elsewhere to raise spending on defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore has always been an ardent supporter of international law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But we have also believed in self-sufficiency in defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have never relied on others to take care of our security.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have invested fully in our own security.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If anything, the global situation validates our prudent approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In today’s world, many countries are at risk of not having enough resources to secure themselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Third, how should Singapore navigate the current global situation?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Over the past 60 years, Singapore has made significant achievements in our development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Nevertheless, even in the face of such uncertainty and an increasinglyfragmented world order, Singapore is not helpless.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have always believed in "preparing umbrellas before it rains".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: While our development has benefited from a relatively stable and harmonious international environment, we have never counted on long-lasting favourable external conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The preparations we have made in the past are now clearly of practical value and will serve us in good stead as we seek progress against headwinds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I have mentioned earlier that we have built up the capability to defend ourselves, as well as the resources for a rainy day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have also invested in building up our national identity and maintaining domestic cohesion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Changes in the external environment will present new challenges to our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singaporeans may have different views on global developments, and we may be subject to hostile information campaigns aimed at influencing domestic opinion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have prepared for these eventualities by putting in laws and regulations, as well as national education.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We maintain friendly and close-knit collaboration with immediate neighbours, including Malaysia and Indonesia; and uphold ASEAN centrality in our engagement of the region.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In a "might makes right" world, we should all the more broaden our network of friends and deepen our positive collaboration with like-minded countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is the rainy day we have prepared for – perhaps a long rainy season.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We need to stay vigilant and navigate with care, in order to seize new opportunities in fast-changing circumstances while mitigating risks.

speaker: The Chairman
text: You can still ask them towards the end, but if you have any now?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: However, beyond the risks and the threats, what opportunities can Singapore seize in this new environment?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: How is the Government positioning us to be able to benefit from these changes?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: For instance, as the global power dynamic shifts, smaller and medium-size countries may be open to seeking closer economic and security ties with Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Is the Government stepping up its outreach to these nations by expanding its network of overseas missions and trade offices?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: However, he did not address how we plan to reduce the risk of over dependence on them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Does the Government have a plan for that?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Lastly, I think the Minister did not respond to my cut about the public diplomacy front.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: How is MFA stepping up the public diplomacy front and using that to be able to explain to Singaporeans about our strategic interest?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The last supplementary question we will handle later, because my colleague, Second Minister Maliki, has not spoken yet.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But let me focus on the first part of the Member's question.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: As I said just now, I spent a lot of time making the point that this is a period of great change and great danger.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But I hope you also glean from my speech that this is not a call for pessimism, because there are opportunities.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And it just so happens that these three revolutions interlock with one another.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In fact, they are feeding and accelerating with one another.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I made the plea that even as we protect Team Singapore, we take a longer-term view to supplement Team Singapore so that we can exploit the full opportunities in frontier technologies.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I have also explained that because of the lack of trust and the contestation and the desperate need for each big power to get ahead of the other, because they are worried that these leads will be exponential, making sure that our paradigm in which we operate Singapore, open to all powers, big, medium and small, that this paradigm is under pressure.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And I also tried to explain the way we make it work is to be open, transparent, fair and to play it straight with all parties.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am acknowledging that it is more difficult.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Everyone will say they are not trying to force us to make choices, but they would rather that we lean more towards one way or the other.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Nevertheless, because we have national interest to have access to these technologies, it is important for us to maintain that reputation, and not just reputation, but in actual operation – probity, transparency and reliability.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, if a foreign company subject to rules which prevail outside Singapore operates here, it must not use its association with us to engage in subterfuge deception or backdoor channels for commercial advantage.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, it calls for a very delicate, agile but at the same time consistent, approach.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If we can do this, we will continue to have access to frontier technologies where we will have an advantage.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Having said that, I also went through in my speech to say do not give up on multilateralism and international law.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But I believe there are still many countries out there, like us, who want that system to work, and even though we no longer have the patronage or the support or the underwriting of major powers that used to do it, we can still make common cause.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, I am not giving up on that.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Basically, the fundamental point is great danger, but once in a lifetime opportunities are opening.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Do not give up our brand and the way we do things openly, transparently, competently, reliably and with trust and openness.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If we can do that, I am confident we can seize the opportunities ahead.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Chairman, Singapore has been in the forefront of providing humanitarian assistance to those who have been displaced because of the conflict between Israel and Hamas.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Thus far, Singapore has sent its seven tranches of humanitarian aid, and the country has pledged that it can do more if required.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: In the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict, our commitment to providing humanitarian aid is commendable, but can we do more to help de-escalate the situation?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Can we leverage our diplomatic standing, whether through ASEAN, the UN or bilateral engagement to encourage restraint and dialogue.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Can the Minister please share his views on the possibility of an expanded role for Singapore in helping to resolve this crisis?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Chairman, Minister Vivian earlier reiterated that Singapore has consistently supported a negotiated two two state solution for Israel and Palestine.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Through the enhanced technical assistance package, nearly 800 Palestinian officials have benefited from our capacity building efforts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: As part of these fundraising efforts at a local level, M³@Pasir Ris Punggol is actively engaging the community across various activities planned throughout the month.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Given the evolving geopolitical landscape, including shifts in the US and the Gulf States responses, what more can Singapore do to support humanitarian relief, reconstruction and diplomatic efforts for stability and peace in Gaza?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: MFA has said on several occasions that Singapore supports the right of Palestinian people to a homeland of their own.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Singapore delivered not one, or two, but a total of six to seven tranches of humanitarian aid for Gaza in January 2025.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Singapore has also provided technical assistance to enhance the Palestinian Authority's capacity for administration and reconstruction.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But I believe that we can do our part, to countries that suffered due to war.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I understand that under the Singapore Cooperation Programme (SCP), we have provided technical assistance to many other developing countries to help these countries with human resource development.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Has Singapore rendered such technical assistance under the SCP to the Palestinian Authority?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What kind of help has Singapore provided, and is it sufficient?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The Gulf region is an important partner for Singapore in energy, finance and investment, with growing collaboration in technology, education and sustainable development.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Our warm relations are underpinned by shared interests in stability, economic progress and global peace.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Recent developments in the trade and financial sectors underscore the potential for Singapore to engage with Gulf countries in sectors such as agriculture, finance and trade, leveraging existing agreements and market dynamics.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: What is the state of Singapore's relations with the Gulf States?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In this regard, amid the ongoing humanitarian crisis in Gaza, Singapore stands in solidarity with the Palestinian civilians affected and has actively contributed to humanitarian efforts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: We have provided aid through organisations like the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) and the Singapore Red Cross to support urgent medical and food supplies.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Singapore has consistently called for the immediate cessation of violence, respect for international law, and a just and lasting resolution.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Moving forward, with the latest tranche of humanitarian aid, Singapore shows commitment in working with Gulf partners and the international community to contribute to a future of peace and stability for the region.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: We should be proud as Singaporeans because we, collectively as a nation, has contributed comparably or indeed more than that by countries in our region alone.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: With the latest temporary ceasefire agreement, what else is Singapore doing to address the situation in Gaza beyond humanitarian aid assistance and, in particular, on any diplomatic channels?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, geopolitical and geo-economic contestation among the major powers is fast becoming the norm on the international stage.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As the contest heats up, it is inevitable that Singapore, as one of the most market-orientated open economies in the world, gets caught up in the crossfire of any such contestation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: One of the methods which has been widely publicised in recent times is the presence of foreign actors that seek to undermine trust in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This, in part, is to seed dissention and discontent domestically to ultimately sway or influence our foreign policy decisions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: While the Government has taken steps to address this legislatively, perhaps more can be done to keep Singaporeans better informed of such insidious intentions by foreign actors.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In this context, I invite the Minister to share how the MFA can play its part to help Singaporeans become more aware of and resilient against such foreign actors who attempt to undermine trust in Singapore's foreign policy decisions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, in our increasingly complex external environment, where information flows freely and narratives can be shaped by foreign actors, Singaporeans risk being influenced by interests that may run counter to our nation's well-being, worse still becoming useful idiots to foreign causes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To safeguard against this, MFA must play a crucial role in keeping our citizens well-informed about our foreign policy principles, core national interests and the broader geopolitical context.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By communicating openly through regular updates, public briefings and community engagements, MFA ensures that Singaporeans understand how our foreign policy decisions are made and why they matter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This knowledge strengthens our national resilience against attempts at foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Beyond that, I hope MFA can share how it partners with other agencies to develop media literacy programmes and help Singaporeans evaluate information and detect malicious campaigns.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, President Tharman recently made a State Visit to India, affirming the warm and longstanding relations between our two countries, as we commemorate the 60th anniversary of diplomatic relations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore and India enjoy strong bilateral economic relations and cooperation in many sectors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: India is set to be one of the fastest-growing economies in the world.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: President Tharman and President Murmu discussed cooperation in areas such as semiconductors, industrial park development, as well as the green and digital economies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Minister share his assessment of Singapore's relations with India, how we will strengthen our people-to-people ties, and what we are doing to deepen our economic ties with India, especially in areas such as the green and digital economies?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: India is one of the first countries who recognised Singapore as an independent country.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: It is the country with the largest population in the world, and we enjoy excellent relationship with India.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Besides our high-level exchanges and economic cooperation, what other areas are we working on to improve the bilateral cooperation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Given its dynamic geopolitical landscape, Singapore must stay engaged to safeguard our interests and contribute to regional stability.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore has long maintained good relations with the region.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Given the ongoing conflicts and realignments in the area, how is Singapore working to strengthen its diplomatic cooperation with these countries?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond bilateral ties, what role can Singapore play in fostering dialogue and multilateral collaboration in areas, such as security, energy and humanitarian assistance?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As the Middle East continues to evolve, how will Singapore ensure that our engagement remains relevant, constructive and aligned with our long-term strategic interests?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, the Middle East continues to be a key region of importance for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Minister share an update on how this FTA has enhanced trade and relations between Singapore and the Middle East?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore also maintains good relationships with the countries in North Africa, especially Algeria, Egypt, Morocco and Tunisia.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How is the Ministry working to build stronger links with Arab states like Egypt and Jordan?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What has been the progress of these two initiatives?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has engaged Latin American countries in many areas of cooperation, including trade and investment, science and technology, and education.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How are we deepening our links in facilitating business opportunities in this emerging market?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Likewise, for the FTA with the Southern Common Market (MERCOSUR), which comprises Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, what is the update on our areas of cooperation so far?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Ministry had shared in the past that Singapore was looking into initiatives with our Latin American partners on the digital economy, food security and carbon credits collaboration.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Africa is an emerging market offering many business and non-economic opportunities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How has our engagement with countries in Africa been and what are the initiatives to deepen our links with Africa?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share more about the official visits and areas of collaboration which we will be working on?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we increase mutual understanding and interactions between our people to facilitate further cooperation in trade and investments?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the main areas of trade and investments from Singapore businesses so far; and how are we encouraging more Singapore enterprises to consider venturing into Africa?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, amid increasing geopolitical uncertainties and trade tensions among major powers, forging connections with middle powers can strengthen Singapore's diplomatic, economic and strategic flexibility, as well as foster innovation and cultural exchanges.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Given Singapore's size and geographical position, middle powers can offer diversified trade opportunities and investment channels which are crucial to Singapore's open economy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: However, navigating the diverse interests of middle powers can also be challenging for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: As Minister Balakrishnan had shared in his speech earlier, Singapore has significant partnerships with several European middle powers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: In 2024, there were several high-level exchanges between Singapore and European countries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: These included then-Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's visits to Germany and France in April, the President's Official Visits to Italy and Estonia in June, and the State Visit by Swedish King Carl XVI Gustaf to Singapore in November.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How have these interactions advanced the interests of Singapore, and what can Singapore do to enhance the relationships with European middle powers?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Mr Chairman, we are living in an increasingly uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: As Singapore deals with a more fragmented geopolitical and geoeconomic international environment, there is a need for us to strategically review our multilateral and bilateral engagements.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The major powers will continue to jostle for power, space and relevance.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Under this backdrop, Singapore's position as an "honest broker" on the international stage will surely come under increasing pressure.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: It is, therefore, in Singapore's interests to deepen our engagements with like-minded middle powers.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In this context, can the Minister share how Singapore is working towards building our ties with such like-minded middle powers?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Further, over the years, Singapore has taken steps to strengthen our interests by forging agreements in Trade, Economic Partnerships, the Digital Economy and even the Green Economy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Given the importance of the Digital Economy in the future, I invite the Minister to also share how the EUSDTA will enhance our partnership and cooperation with the EU and, in the larger context, chart the foreign policy objectives of Singapore in the future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How are we enhancing bilateral cooperation with both countries and in Asia overall?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: While I am happy and fully support the nomination, I would like ask the Minister to share on the Government's thinking behind her nomination and how this nomination would contribute our part towards the upholding of international rule of law?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Since Independence, Singapore has actively participated in many international agencies like the UN and many other platforms, like WHO and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: For a small nation state, international rule of law means a lot to us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: It is in Singapore's interest to steadfastly advance the international rule of law.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: The ICJ is the UN's key judicial organ and it plays a vital role in upholding international laws and agreements, and in the adjudication of legal dispute between countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I am sure Ambassador Rena Lee's impeccable reputation and credentials, as well as the international recognition of Singapore as having among the best judiciary and legal systems in the world will stand her in good stead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: We wish her all the best in the election.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Since our Independence, Singapore has maintained the importance of capacity-building as a pillar of regional cooperation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It serves as a platform to provide technical assistance to the world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, the SCP's initiatives are equally beneficial to us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We get to share and also learn about best practices in various areas, from public governance to global sustainability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As we celebrate SG60, global challenges remain uncertain whether in the realm of climate change, sustainability or cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is an ever-growing need to gather our efforts towards deeper and more targeted technical assistance to areas where our counterparts need our expertise the most.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could MFA share how Singapore intends to enhance its capacity-building efforts to address these emerging challenges?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Chairman, Singapore has made very significant contributions to various regions and the world over the years through SCP.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Specifically, can I ask how has Singapore supported the capacity-building efforts of fellow small states through the programme?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Chairman, we have seen a surge in overseas travel as Singaporeans continue to embrace travelling in the new post-pandemic norm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: But what happens when help is needed in places where we lack consular presence?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Plagued by heightened global tensions, we must remember that conflicts can happen in any country, unprovoked and unexpectedly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It is, hence, imperative that our consular efforts can promise operational capabilities in which country Singaporeans might find themselves in.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Chairman, these days, when Singaporeans prepare to travel overseas, besides our world's number one passport, foreign currency and travel insurance, they also check – e-registered with MFA already or not?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: The consular services provided by MFA have served Singaporeans well and over the years.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Chairman, in an era where social media influences how we consume news, foreign policy is no longer confined to the realm of diplomats; it is actively debated in homes, classrooms and online forums.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Yet, global issues are becoming increasingly polarised, from the ongoing Israel-Palestine conflict to climate policies and shifting geopolitical alliances.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Misinformation spreads quickly and public opinion can be shaped in moments.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Many Singaporeans seek a clearer understanding of how our foreign policy decisions are made and a platform to voice their views.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: If we fail to engage proactively in the digital space, we risk allowing narratives that are inaccurate or misaligned with Singapore's best interests.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Ultimately, foreign policy is about safeguarding our nation in an unpredictable world.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Chairman, the ubiquitous influence of social media has shaped interactions and discussions on every conceivable topic and issue, including a country's foreign policy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Singaporeans, living in one of the most digitised countries in the world, are more engaged than ever in discussions about our foreign policy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: All of us are keenly aware that as a small nation, an open economy highly dependent on international trade, developments in our region and further afield globally have a significant impact on us.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: While we should continue to encourage and support the public to keep up to date with current affairs and learn more about foreign developments, we must constantly remind Singaporeans to keep a balanced perspective, and to be open to and be tolerant of different views and interpretations.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: This is crucial, considering that we are a multiracial and multi-religious community.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: We must be cognisant of the complex factors shaping different global developments and trust that our foreign service departments and officers have weighed in and considered the best positions and options available to us in Singapore's best interests.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Hence, most importantly, we must remain united as Singaporeans and not be swayed by foreign influences.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How does MFA strike a balance between maintaining a cohesive national position and acknowledging the diversity of opinions among Singaporeans on international issues?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Chairman, Singaporeans are increasingly interested in foreign policy, particularly as global developments become more complex and interconnected.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: The ease of obtaining news and exchanging views and opinions online has led to more Singaporeans reading and discussing international current affairs and the role and position of our foreign policy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Would the Ministry share what it is doing to build and deepen Singaporeans' understanding of the key tenets of our foreign policy, including important considerations and constraints, in layman terms which are easier to comprehend?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: How is MFA adapting its engagement strategies to increase understanding of Singapore's foreign policy fundamentals?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: How would the Ministry highlight to our citizens that good foreign policy contributes to the well-being of Singapore and Singaporeans and secure domestic support for our foreign policy decisions?

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Neil Parekh asked about the situation in Gaza, what Singapore has done to address the situation, and what more we can do to support a de-escalation of the conflict.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked how Singapore has supported the Palestinian Authority through the Singapore Cooperation Programme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Please allow me to take these questions together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: I will respond in Malay. :   Chairman, for the past 16 months, we are witnessing a terrible humanitarian tragedy in Gaza through heart wrenching images.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: There is a Malay saying "berat mata memandang, berat lagi bahu yang memikul" (it is hard for the person seeing, it is even harder for the person experiencing) We saw not only the destruction of lives but also the devastation of homes and communities in Gaza.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: People in Gaza lack access to basic necessities like water, food, electricity, and medicine.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The situation is even more critical with the advent of the holy month of Ramadan as the people of Gaza observe their fast without the basic humanitarian essentials that are desperately needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The ceasefire agreement provides a ray of hope for the people of Gaza towards the peace that they dream of.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Phase one of the ceasefire and hostage release agreement has formally ended.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We urge all parties to quickly come to an agreement on Phase two.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In the meantime, Singapore's position is that humanitarian assistance to the people of Gaza must be allowed access to continue to alleviate the humanitarian crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We are deeply concerned over Israel's latest decision to halt the entry of goods and supplies into the Gaza Strip.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We urge all parties to do their utmost to reach an agreement on a permanent ceasefire and the release of all hostages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Singaporeans recognise the deep complexities of the Israel-Palestine conflict, and this conflict will become even more complex if we consider the broader geopolitical realities in the Middle East.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Chairman, this conflict is a long-standing feud going back decades, if not centuries, involving multiple state and non-state actors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Importantly, we need to know that the conflict is not a clash between people of different faiths.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is a political battle for territory, self-determination, identity, and human dignity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Singapore's approach towards the conflict is one that is long-standing and consistent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: While we have highlighted Singapore's approach many times before, please allow me to once again explain in detail the key tenets guiding our position on the Israel-Palestine conflict.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: A two-state solution means that both Israelis and Palestinians mutually recognise each other’s right to exist as a state and to live alongside each other in peace and security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Second, our position on the negotiated two-state solution means that Singapore has consistently supported the right of the Palestinian people to a homeland of their own.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: However, we first need to be sure that such a move will facilitate progress towards peace and a negotiated two-state solution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This means that there will need to be an effective Palestinian government that categorically rejects terrorism and is prepared to accept Israel's right to exist, just like the existence of Palestine that they desire.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We have also rejected illegal Israeli settlement activities, which make it much harder to arrive at a viable two-state solution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We have also called out violations of international law and unilateral actions that attempt to change the status quo.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We have stated this position on past occasions in Parliament.

speaker: The Second Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is also reflected through our votes at the UN.

speaker: The Chairman
text: (In English) Do we have copies of Minister's handouts?

speaker: The Chairman
text: I think in the meantime, if it is possible for you to proceed with your speech?

speaker: The Chairman
text: It bears remembering that over 1,200 Israeli and foreign civilians were killed during Hamas' terror attacks on 7 October 2023.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Many were ordinary men, women and children going about their daily lives.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Hamas also captured 251 individuals, including ASEAN nationals and held them hostage.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There cannot be any justifications whatsoever for these acts.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Fifth, while countries have the right of self-defence, their actions must comply with international law, including international humanitarian law.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Following the 7 October 2023 attacks, we affirmed Israel's right to self-defence.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have firmly stated this matter in our discussions with Israel.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This is not merely a matter of principles or a theoretical issue and not something that could never happen to us.

speaker: The Chairman
text: These principles strike at the heart of Singapore's existence as an independent and sovereign country.

speaker: The Chairman
text: As a small country – and we hope that other countries will agree – we cannot brook any entity that denies Singapore's right to exist or seeks to cause our country and people harm.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Some Singaporeans want the Government to go beyond the provision of humanitarian assistance to Gaza.

speaker: The Chairman
text: They urge the Government to take a stronger stance against Israel.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The Government feels that this is not the most productive approach.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We understand that Singaporeans have a diversity of opinions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Some have been quite active and assertive in expressing their views, including to their Members of Parliament.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It is crucial to understand that Singapore's approach to foreign policy is consistent and long-standing.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We act based on what is in our national interests.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It is not based on us choosing one side over another.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We must remain clear-eyed and not allow our emotions to dictate the manner in which Singapore conducts our foreign policy, either on this conflict or on any other international issue.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Chairman, as we continue to understand the ongoing conflict, it is worth noting that all Arab states which have diplomatic relations with Israel prior to the 7 October 2023 attacks have not severed ties with Israel.

speaker: The Chairman
text: They are instead focused on active diplomacy and have taken constructive steps to alleviate the suffering of civilians in Gaza through humanitarian aid.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Other countries, just like Singapore, have taken this position because we recognize that adopting drastic measures, such as severing ties with Israel, would only serve to further destabilize the region.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are all of the view that engagement, rather than isolation, is the best path forward to keep the prospects of a two-state solution alive for Israel and Palestine.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Through active diplomacy, Singapore continues to find opportunities to engage and encourage all relevant parties to pursue a longer-term solution that will bring about regional peace and stability.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Last March, Minister Vivian Balakrishan visited the Middle East, including Israel and the Palestinian Territories, with a cross-party parliamentary delegation.

speaker: The Chairman
text: During my visits to Egypt, Jordan, and Bahrain over the past four months, I engaged various Arab Ministers to better understand their concerns and the outlook for Gaza.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It is clear that they remain concerned about the escalating tensions in the Middle East and the need for a resolution to the long-standing Israeli-Palestinian conflict, through a two-state solution and the guarantee of security for both sides.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Their position is the same as Singapore's – that is, we need to keep the lines of communication with the Israelis and Palestinians open.

speaker: The Chairman
text: At the same time, we are realistic about the role Singapore can play.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We must accept that a positive breakthrough in Israel-Palestine relations will only be possible if leaders on both sides have the will and courage to set aside differences, be prepared to make progress together, and be prepared to make concessions – all these will lead to a lasting two-state solution.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It is also crucial for there to be political stability and strong domestic support within Israel and Palestine for the peace process to succeed.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We continue to urge the Israelis and Palestinians to resume direct negotiations and to refrain from any unilateral actions, especially violence, which would be unhelpful to the peace process.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In the meantime, what Singapore and Singaporeans can do is to channel our focus and resources in a productive manner, especially towards humanitarian assistance.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Since the current Gaza conflict took place, Singaporeans from all walks of life have donated significantly and sincerely, both in cash and in kind, towards the provision of critical humanitarian assistance to Gaza.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This stems from a desire to do what we can to alleviate the suffering of civilians in Gaza.

speaker: The Chairman
text: During my visit to the Egyptian Red Cresent in November 2023, I participated in the packing of essential items destined for Gaza.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Just last month, we sent off our seventh tranche of aid comprising food, as well as medical and hygiene supplies, using the RSAF's Multi-Role Tanker Transport (MRTT) aircraft, with the assistance of the Jordan Hashemite Charity Organisation (JHCO).

speaker: The Chairman
text: Singapore will continue to do what we can to contribute bilaterally and in partnership with others in the Middle East.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I hope Singaporeans will continue to donate generously to fundraising initiatives for Gaza, including the Rahmatan Lil Alamin Foundation's (RLAF's) current fundraiser during Ramadan with M3, launched just last week.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am heartened at the support we have received thus far.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am confident that Singaporeans will continue to support this fundraiser along with the Singapore Red Cross' ongoing fundraising project.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Beyond humanitarian aid, we remain committed to supporting the Palestinian Authority's human capital development efforts through the Singapore Cooperation Programme, including the Enhanced Technical Assistance Package (ETAP).

speaker: The Chairman
text: In redoubling our efforts to provide technical assistance to the Palestinian people, we hope that this will contribute towards their preparation for eventual statehood.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Chairman, the Government acknowledges that this is a conflict with strong emotional resonance amongst Singaporeans, especially our Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Many experience anger due to their sympathy for the innocent victims.

speaker: The Chairman
text: But we must not allow ourselves to be influenced by those who seek to use this conflict to incite violence and hatred and to divide us.

speaker: The Chairman
text: More importantly, we must not allow an issue like this to be politicised.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am glad to note that Members of this House, regardless of political affiliation, understand the complexity of the situation in Gaza and have supported the Government's approach following the 7 October attacks.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In fact, MP Gerald Giam was part of Minister Vivian's delegation to Israel and the Palestinian Territories to see the situation first-hand, including the significance of our position and approach towards this conflict.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Chairman, Singaporeans, including the Malay/Muslim community, have shown maturity in the way we manage this situation.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We mutually respect each other' views that may differ, but we are prepared to place Singapore’s interests ahead and continue to protect the social cohesion and stability in Singapore.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The Singapore Government will continue to actively engage Singaporeans to explain our positions on geopolitical issues including the fundamental interests and principles that underpin our foreign policy to ensure peace and stability for Singaporeans. : Mr Chairman, allow me to continue my speech in English.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I just spoke about the humanitarian assistance that Singapore and Singaporeans are providing to the civilians who are suffering in Gaza.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have been in close coordination with countries, such as Egypt, Jordan and the UAE, to better understand the priorities on the ground and the type of essential supplies that are needed, to ensure that our aid reaches those who need them most.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The crisis in Gaza illustrates the importance of building goodwill and trust with our partners in the Middle East.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Continuing to do so will allow us to better navigate complex regional geopolitics, as well as to seize emerging opportunities for joint collaboration.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Dr Wan Rizal asked about Singapore's efforts to deepen relations with the Middle East.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Saudi Arabia is a major player in the Middle East and is undergoing rapid socioeconomic changes under the Vision 2030 masterplan.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This new platform will allow both leaders to chart the strategic direction of our bilateral relations.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The UAE is our largest trading partner in the region.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Last October, we welcomed Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi His Highness Sheikh Khaled Bin Mohamed Bin Zayed to Singapore.

speaker: The Chairman
text: With Qatar, we share mutual interests and enjoy strong cooperation.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Oman is an emerging market that presents opportunities for Singaporean companies.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister Vivian Balakrishnan spoke about the changing geopolitical realities confronting Singapore and the future ahead.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Established global norms, which served as the bedrock of the rules-based multilateral system, are being challenged.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There are increasing areas of contestation and a multipolar order is emerging.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It has become even more important for Singaporeans to remain united to weather the oncoming storms.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Having strong and united domestic support for Singapore's foreign policy will facilitate MFA's mission of advancing Singapore's interests abroad.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We do this by: first, fostering coalitions of like-minded partners to advance common goals, such as upholding international law and multilateralism; second, ensuring that our voice is heard in developing international norms and rules, through our active participation and leadership of international organisations, such as UN, International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the World Intellectual Property Office (WIPO); and third, by laying the groundwork for deeper and more sustained engagements with our international partners.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Some Singaporeans have asked how Singapore's relations with international partners bring material benefits to them.

speaker: The Chairman
text: While these benefits may not always be immediately visible or tangible, fostering friendly relations with other countries allows us to: one, ensure Singapore's continued peace and prosperity, by ensuring that others have a stake in our survival; and two, position Singapore at the forefront of emerging and frontier areas of growth, including shaping new norms with like-minded countries.

speaker: The Chairman
text: To do so, we must remain nimble in navigating the uncertain geopolitical environment by being relevant to our partners.

speaker: The Chairman
text: By building new links and maintaining bridges with friends from all around the world, Singapore is able to advance our interests and remain relevant and trusted in today's complex international environment.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked how Singapore has been deepening relations with emerging markets and India.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Last year was a busy year in our engagement of Latin America.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Brazil held the G20 Presidency and Peru chaired APEC.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Many Singapore leaders and officials attended various meetings and met their foreign counterparts in that region.

speaker: The Chairman
text: For instance, Brazil is already an important source of frozen chicken and beef.

speaker: The Chairman
text: These agreements will not only further grow our trade with Latin America, but also strengthen Singapore's food resilience and add diversity to the range of products and services available to us, including carbon credits.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are also looking to deepen our links with Africa.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Last year, I visited Cote d'Ivoire and Nigeria, two major political and economic powerhouses in Africa, to engage key leaders and to understand their priorities and where Singapore can fit in.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This will help to facilitate Singapore companies interested in exploring commercial opportunities in Africa and build goodwill and support for Singapore.

speaker: The Chairman
text: India remains an important strategic and economic partner.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will continue to leverage the India-Singapore Ministerial Roundtable platform to deliver concrete and mutually beneficial outcomes in areas, such as digitalisation, skills development, advanced manufacturing and connectivity.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will also build up our relations at the regional and state levels.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In stepping up our engagement of these emerging markets and regions, MFA seeks to expand cooperation in new areas for mutual benefit and to build goodwill and support for Singapore bilaterally and in international bodies.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This will put Singapore in a good position to seize opportunities and work together with our partners.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Don Wee, Mr Chong Kee Hiong and Ms Joan Pereira also asked about Singapore’s relations with our neighbours.

speaker: The Chairman
text: While we look for new opportunities further afield, Singapore’s success and future remain inextricably tied to Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Chairman
text: With Malaysia, there is strong political will to work together on a win-win basis.

speaker: The Chairman
text: With Brunei, we are building our special relationship, and building upon that relationship, to jointly explore new and emerging areas, like sustainable development, education, public sector capacity, as well as food safety and resilience.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Singapore and Indonesia have made substantive progress in existing and emerging areas, such as renewable energy, human capital development and education.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are working with Indonesia to jointly advance our green transition journey.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Given President Prabowo Subianto’s commitment to developing Indonesia’s human potential, we also plan to deepen education exchanges and human capital development cooperation.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Similarly, our cooperation with Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Cambodia and Laos is growing.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have been pioneers on the financial front with Thailand, having established a cross-border fast digital payment link-up and a Depository Receipts Linkage between our stock exchanges.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Singapore and Vietnam will upgrade our ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and our businesses remain excited about Vietnam’s growth potential.

speaker: The Chairman
text: To date, we have established 18 Vietnam-Singapore Industrial Parks and there is interest to do more.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are also working with Cambodia, Laos, the Philippines and Thailand on renewable energy and carbon markets.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The prospects and future of our neighbourhood are bright.

speaker: The Chairman
text: With a population of nearly 700 million, a young and dynamic workforce, healthy GDP growth and rapid urbanisation, ASEAN has tremendous potential to be a key node of economic growth for the world.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Miss Rachel Ong had asked how Singapore can work with fellow ASEAN member states to enhance economic integration in the region.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are taking tangible steps to realise a sustainable and secure future by developing the ASEAN Power Grid.

speaker: The Chairman
text: A more interconnected region will better enable each country to meet rising energy demands and remain resilient in the face of potential disruptions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Maintaining peace and stability in Southeast Asia is crucial to our collective goal of building a more dynamic, integrated and resilient ASEAN.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This is why we continue to pay close attention to Myanmar.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It is unfortunate that there has been limited progress in Myanmar’s implementation of the ASEAN Five-Point Consensus since it was agreed to in April 2021.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Our prohibition includes dual-use items which have been assessed to have potential military application and where there is serious risk that they may be used to inflict violence against unarmed civilians.

speaker: The Chairman
text: At the same time, it is important to note that the Singapore Government does not seek to block legitimate trade with Myanmar.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have been very careful to avoid inadvertently causing greater hardship for the Myanmar people.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin and Ms Sylvia Lim have asked how Singapore and ASEAN can facilitate progress in Myanmar.

speaker: The Chairman
text: ASEAN will continue to address the issue in line with the Five-Point Consensus based on the decisions made by our ASEAN Leaders.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Singapore will continue to support Malaysia as the current ASEAN Chair, and its Special Envoy, and other external partners to facilitate peace and national reconciliation while respecting the fundamental principle of non-interference.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Singapore will also continue to support ASEAN’s efforts to provide humanitarian assistance through the ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance on Disaster Management.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The situation in Myanmar is complicated and any enduring political solution will have to come from within Myanmar itself.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The only way to achieve a sustainable and peaceful national reconciliation is through constructive dialogue among all the key stakeholders.

speaker: The Chairman
text: To buffer against global headwinds and uncertainty, it has become even more critical for Singapore to broaden and diversify our global network of partners and friends.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Fortunately, countries are eager to deepen cooperation with Singapore because of our reputation as a reliable and trustworthy partner.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We must be brave and nimble to seize new opportunities, just as our forefathers once did.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The world has become a more dangerous and uncertain place, but we have good reason to be confident about Singapore’s future.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Chairman, I wish to thank the various Members for filing cuts about MFA's engagement with like-minded partners, and I believe these have been addressed in Minister Vivian Balakrishnan and Minister Mohamad Maliki's earlier speeches.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Chairman, please allow me to address the questions on safeguarding Singapore's interest on the international stage, our capacity building efforts, consular assistance and MFA's engagement of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Poh Li San and Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked how Singapore stays ahead in emerging areas and why we nominated Ambassador Rena Lee for the ICJ candidature.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We remain actively engaged on emerging issues at multilateral fora like the UN.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Given the current geopolitical environment, it is critical that Singapore contributes to the advancement of international law through deeds.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Elections will be keenly contested, but we will do our best to support Ambassador Lee as we believe she will contribute significantly to the ICJ.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan and Mr Desmond Choo have asked about Singapore’s capacity-building efforts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Supporting human resource development of fellow developing countries through the Singapore Cooperation Programme (SCP) remains MFA’s priority.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We are committed to do more for Timor-Leste under the SCP, to help them prepare to join ASEAN.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We also have technical assistance packages for members of the Forum of Small States, which Minister Vivian Balakrishnan had mentioned, and fellow small island developing countries.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Xie Yao Quan have asked about MFA’s consular assistance efforts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Our Missions around the world extended assistance under difficult circumstances, for example, during the severe flooding in Hainan and the earthquake in Vanuatu.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We urge Singaporeans to continue to e-register with us.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We have also leveraged technology to help us deliver consular assistance more quickly and effectively.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Poh Li San, Ms Joan Pereira, Miss Rachel Ong and Mr Gerald Giam have asked how we were engaging Singaporeans on foreign policy issues.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: By introducing foreign policy concepts early, we empower young Singaporeans to have an interest in Singapore’s approach to global issues.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Even when views diverge, respectful dialogue is key.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We aim to make foreign policy understandable, including through social media, and this is on top of the talks and dialogues that we already do.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: A shared sense of responsibility and vision ensures that we can face global challenges with confidence and cohesion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The first is: pulling together the different threads of multilateralism, it is quite clear that the current US administration has moved away from the multilateral approach.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But what seems to emerge is that many other countries, including Europe, Japan, and even China has said it is bringing its disputes to the WTO.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: So, is it possible that there are divergent currents, and there are, in fact, many countries which still believe in multilateralism, and it would still be possible to work on the positive views towards multilateralism and build more networks for Singapore, which I think we are already doing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The second is: I am grateful to Minister Maliki for sharing the principled approach we have taken in relation to Palestine, and for reminding this House that we have taken a strong view against the illegal actions taken by Israel in the occupied territories.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: One of the issues that many agencies providing aid are facing is that aid is not actually reaching the recipients.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What has Singapore's experience been with aid reaching the recipients, and if we have been successful, what has helped with that?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: There are still many countries which realise that it is in our enlightened long-term interest to support multilateralism and international law, and the Member has just mentioned the list would include Europe, it will include Southeast Asia, and even in the longer run, certainly South America and Africa.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But we also need to be realistic that if the big powers, with a lack of strategic trust and trying to stay ahead, are willing to take liberties with multilateralism, or maybe the other way I would express it is that they are not willing to be restricted and tied down by the restraints of multilateralism or international law, and given their current imperative to stay ahead of one another, it will be very difficult to operate.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And that is the point I am making.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, it does not mean we give up.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In fact, it means the rest of us need to double down, need to do our best to support the WTO and WHO and to support the UN and to continue to make the point that the UN Charter is essential, and that if the UN goes the way of the League of Nations, then we are in very, very dangerous territory.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Are we in a pre-World War I phase?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Which was characterised by empires reaching their limits, globalisation in an empire way was coming to an end.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Then, you had World War I, at least four empires were destroyed by it.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But even in the aftermath of World War I, the Treaty of Versailles, the reparations; the territorial boundary redrawing in Germany; the Great Depression in the 1929 onwards, you had a world with beggar-thy-neighbour policies, depression, grievance and the domestic rise of Nazism and Fascism – all the isms.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: That really set the stage for World War II.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Every additional dollar generated in the world, 40 cents came back to America.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It was worth its while to underwrite that liberal world order that we have enjoyed for the past 80 years.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We are no longer in that kind of climate.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: As I said, this is a geo-strategic climate change.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is not just a change of weather.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: To the maximum extent, continue to hold fast to our principles.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But understand that it is not business as usual.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I think the Member had the other question on Israel.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It has been difficult for aid to reach the people in Gaza, a combination of reasons.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The convoys get mobbed the moment they cross over because there is chaos and no security.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We ourselves, as Minister Ng Eng Hen has emphasised, we ourselves have considered how can we even deploy medical or humanitarian facilities, but it is not possible to do so safely.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: What we can do is to continue to impress on Israelis that it is in their own interest to facilitate aid deliveries.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But I am afraid they have prioritised their security and other considerations over that.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I note that even in the last few days, there has been further hurdles to delivery of assistance.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: To the extent that our voice is heard, we will add to that chorus that says, it is in Israel's interest to make sure aid flows to the people who need help.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have a clarification on Myanmar and ASEAN.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Under the ASEAN Five-Point Consensus, there seems to be a heavy reliance on the special envoy being appointed to possibly mediate between the parties, to visit the parties in Myanmar.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I wonder whether that is something that we are pushing for or has been considered.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I think these are all ideas which can be considered.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But again, in the spirit of being realistic, Myanmar is a very, very difficult challenge.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And the problems do not just go back to 2021, when the coup was launched.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It goes back to the fact that they have never yet been able to truly constitute a single nation out of the diversity that encompasses the totality of Myanmar.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They have not yet been able to work out the political formula to bring people together, to bring all the different elements of state together into a balance which is constructive and positive.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I say all this to illustrate that they have not even got past the fundamental nation building exercise.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The coup is just one more symptom of that fundamental problem.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The other point you also need to realise is that we must understand by now, I have seen no historical example of an external interference riding in, conquering even and building a nation.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Having elections does not solve any political problem if you have not got the values and that spirit to achieve workable compromises.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: From my interactions in the past – I have not gone there since 2021, but certainly, from my past interactions with Myanmar leaders across the spectrum, I found it is very difficult to get them together.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Because if we get impatient, what are our alternatives?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I guarantee the Member, it will not work.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: At the end of the day, these fractured countries, their leaders need to arrive at the appropriate political compromise and to create a nation out of very disparate segments who, unfortunately, because so much blood has been shed, have a lot of stored grievances.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am sure the Member is also speaking from direct experience.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is heartbreaking for them and their relatives.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But be very, very careful not to make things worse.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am sorry I do not have a quick solution for Myanmar, except that to the extent that they are willing to compromise.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I believe we currently only have one resident mission in Sub-Saharan Africa.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Are there plans to open up more Embassies, High Commissions or Trade Offices in growing and influential African countries, like Nigeria and Kenya, as well as in South America?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Beyond consular assistance, this could be another step towards diversifying our economic and diplomatic interests beyond the major powers, which is what I raised in my cut as well.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I believe Mr Gerald Giam used to be an MFA officer.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: He understands the challenges with regard to manpower.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I think if we are able to have more resources, we will do more.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: But the reality is that resources are limited.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We ensure that when we decide to establish or open a new Embassy or a new Mission in any city or any country, it is because we see there is potential for a relationship to be established at a higher level.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, we start off with ascertaining the potential for collaboration with a particular country.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We do have non-resident ambassadors (NRAs) already appointed in several African countries.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: The non-resident ambassadors have done an excellent job for us.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: They started looking at various areas for collaboration, established relationships with key leaders in those African countries.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I am pretty sure when the time comes, when we see the potential being a lot more real, we will then be able to make those decisions.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: But for now, I want to assure Mr Giam that our NRAs have done an excellent job.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We continue to also have systems where ambassadors in one particular mission are also accredited into another country.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: It does not mean that without a mission, that those countries are not taken care of.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We continue to pay attention to the various accounts or the different countries in the African region, as with any other region, and we continue to assess the extent to which we are able to set up new missions, depending on the resources that are available.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Because it is not only taking away the idea of the rule of law, it is also something along the lines that might is right and big is beautiful.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The Minister alluded to SG60 just now, very briefly, but really, 60 years of a wonderful nation building is not enough.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, from an MFA perspective, what is the plan?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But more seriously, I think historically, Venice as a city-state survived for several centuries.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But actually, in the long run of history, it has not been kind for tiny city-states.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: As a consequence of that, we should be grateful Mr Lee Kuan Yew, Dr Goh Keng Swee, Mr S Rajaratnam decided that the loss of our immediate hinterland does not have to mean that we are cut off from our supplies and economic opportunities.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If you read the speeches in the 1960s, the concept of being a global city, of leapfrogging even our immediate neighbourhood came about.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But in my speech, what I was also trying to say, that concept worked at a very unusual time in global history.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Unusual, because it was Pax Americana characterised by free trade, global supply chains, expansions of multinational enterprises, multilateral organisations, international law.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Can you see how that global environment was so conducive to this fledging, unlikely city-state trying to forge and make a living as a global city?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Fast forward to today, I think our Pioneer leaders managed to capture every gust of wind that was available.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Out of just imagination and gumption, we became a global financial centre.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And then, we also benefited not just because of the rule of law and common law and the fact that our bureaucracy and our legislation fitted quite easily into the British common law, and therefore by extension, even American systems.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Can you see my point that yes, of course, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, once when I was sailing in with him in Marina Bay before it became closed, actually we were looking for where to place the Integrated Resorts.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But as we were sailing in one sunset, I saw this beautiful landscape, I turned to him and Mr Lim Kim San was beside.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I said, "How do you feel, Mr Lee, seeing this wonderful city?" He just looked at me gruffly and said, "Hardworking and disciplined people built all this." No fancy theory.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, yes, hardworking and disciplined people called Singaporeans built all this.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Today, now, 60 years later, I know, I am trying not to be too partisan and too politically, but seriously, I remember Mr Neil Parekh saying last week, if our biggest criticism is that we have been lucky and we got unanticipated high corporate tax revenues because companies have come here and their activities have been successful and we are being criticised for having large, fiscal reserves, well, I appeal to the Opposition.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Given the state of the world today, even the US is wondering how to pay off its national debt.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Do you want to be a net debtor, paying off your debts?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Or are we better off with a significant reserve; and between the return on reserves or corporate tax competing to see which one is bigger, can you see there is great reason to be grateful?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We are going to a more hostile, more difficult environment.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But I am also saying, please do not be pessimistic and do not lose hope because we have strengths.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Having those reserves, having the fiscal strength, the debate which we are having now about the Budget is, I think, unique in the world.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: No one else is facing this luxury, where the Finance Minister, the Prime Minister, can put significant sums in long-term funds to invest in our people, in our infrastructure and to make ourselves future ready.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, I cannot look 600 years, but let us just settle for 10 years.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: What are the opportunities in the next 10 years?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I have said, maybe I am biased, as a doctor, as a surgeon, but I happen to believe digital technologies and AI, biotechnology, because in fact healthcare and biology have now become an extension of digital technologies.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is digital technologies that have enabled the acceleration of the human genome project, it is digital technologies that has enabled us now to solve the issue of protein folding and to create designer molecules, designer drugs.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: There is so much there and we have not even started about editing the human genome.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And green energy, sustainable energy, because guess what?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
